sectionTitle: Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity.
The voltage produced by a cell is dependent upon a number of factors including the type of electrode and electrolyte.
A simple cell can be made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte.
Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage.
In non-rechargeable cells and batteries the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.
Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied.
Students should be able to interpret data for relative reactivity of different metals and evaluate the use of cells.
Students do not need to know details of cells and batteries other than those specified.
Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air. The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference.
The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water.
Hydrogen fuel cells offer a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries.
evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells in comparison with rechargeable cells and batteries
(HT only) write the half equations for the electrode reactions in the hydrogen fuel cell.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know details of cells and batteries other than those specified.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nothing here goes beyond the cells and batteries the specification itself names. Cell chemistry is treated only at the level of 'two different metals in contact with an electrolyte'; the only named battery type is the alkaline battery, and it is used only to make the point the specification makes, that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable. No item asks for the internal chemistry, construction, named electrode materials or reaction equations of any commercial cell (zinc-carbon, lithium-ion, lead-acid, nickel-cadmium), for standard electrode potentials, or for the salt bridge and electrochemical series treatment used at A-level. Where reactivity data are used (q12), they are given in the question as voltages to be interpreted, not recalled.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) write the half equations for the electrode reactions in the hydrogen fuel cell.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Half equations for the fuel cell electrodes appear only in items tagged tier "higher": concepts c19, c20 and c21, misconceptions m17, m18 and m23, and questions q21 and q22. Every Foundation-accessible item about the hydrogen fuel cell asks only for the overall reaction, the products, or the evaluation, never for a half equation. The overall equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is treated as 'both' tier because it is the overall reaction of 4.5.2.2, not an electrode half equation.

concepts.definition: A cell contains chemicals which react to produce electricity. The electricity is not stored inside the cell in advance; it is produced while the reaction between the chemicals is happening, and it lasts only for as long as that reaction can continue.

One of the two conducting pieces, usually metals, that dip into the electrolyte and connect the chemicals in the cell to the external circuit. The type of electrode used is one of the factors the voltage of the cell depends on.

The liquid or solution containing free-moving ions in which the electrodes are placed. It is not simply a means of joining the electrodes: the type of electrolyte is one of the factors that determines the voltage the cell produces.

The potential difference the cell produces, measured with a voltmeter connected across it. It is dependent upon a number of factors, including the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte used. It does not depend on how large the pieces of electrode are.

A cell made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Both conditions matter: the two metals must be different from each other, and they must be in contact with an electrolyte rather than with air or with pure water.
Two or more cells connected together in series. Everyday speech calls a single cell a battery, but in chemistry a battery is the combination of cells, not one cell on its own.

Connecting cells one after another, positive terminal to negative terminal. Cells are connected in series in a battery to provide a greater voltage than a single cell can: the voltages of the individual cells add together.

A cell in which the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up. Once that reactant is gone the cell cannot produce electricity again, and supplying an external current will not restart it.

The everyday battery named by the specification as an example of the non-rechargeable type. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable: when a reactant inside has been used up the battery is finished and must be disposed of or recycled.

A cell that can be recharged because the chemical reactions inside it are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. The reactants are re-formed from the products, so the cell can produce electricity again.

Supplying an external electrical current to a rechargeable cell or battery. The current drives the chemical reactions backwards, turning the products of the discharge reaction back into the reactants. No new chemicals are added to the cell.

When cells are made from pairs of metals in the same electrolyte, the voltage produced depends on how far apart the two metals are in the reactivity series. The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage of the cell.

In a simple cell made from two different metals, the more reactive metal is the negative electrode: it is the metal that loses electrons more readily. Voltage data for pairs of metals can therefore be used to place the metals in order of reactivity.

Weighing up the advantages and disadvantages of a cell for a given job. A non-rechargeable cell is cheap and ready to use but is thrown away once a reactant is used up; a rechargeable cell costs more at first but is used many times, so it produces less waste.

A cell supplied by an external source of fuel, for example hydrogen, and oxygen or air. Because the fuel comes from outside, the cell keeps producing electricity for as long as the fuel and oxygen are supplied, rather than stopping when an internal reactant is used up.

Inside a fuel cell the fuel is oxidised electrochemically rather than burned. The oxidation takes place at an electrode, so the electrons transferred pass through the external circuit, and this produces a potential difference.

concepts.term: Overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell
concepts.definition: The overall reaction involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Water is the only product of the reaction in the cell.

concepts.term: Fuel cells compared with rechargeable batteries
concepts.definition: Hydrogen fuel cells offer a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries. A fuel cell needs no recharging time and keeps working while fuel is supplied, and the only product of the reaction is water; but hydrogen is difficult to store and to distribute safely, and rechargeable batteries can be refilled with energy from any electricity supply.
An equation for what happens at one electrode alone, showing the electrons that are lost or gained. In a half equation both the atoms and the total charge must balance on the two sides.

concepts.term: Negative electrode of the hydrogen fuel cell
concepts.definition: Hydrogen is oxidised, losing electrons: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. The electrons released travel round the external circuit. (In a cell with an alkaline electrolyte the same oxidation is written 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻.)

concepts.term: Positive electrode of the hydrogen fuel cell
concepts.definition: Oxygen is reduced, gaining the electrons that arrive from the circuit: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. (In a cell with an alkaline electrolyte the reduction is written O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.) Adding the two half equations gives the overall reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

misconceptions.question: Where is the electricity in a cell before the cell is connected?
misconceptions.correct: It is not anywhere. Electricity is produced by the reaction once the circuit is complete.
misconceptions.misconception: A cell is a container with electricity already inside it, and using the cell empties out the electricity it was filled with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language treats batteries as things that are full or empty, and diagrams of circuits show charge flowing out of the cell, which invites the picture of a tank being drained.
misconceptions.correction: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity. Until the circuit is complete no current flows and no electricity exists in the cell; when the circuit is closed the reaction between the chemicals produces it.

misconceptions.question: Does changing the electrolyte change the voltage a cell produces?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The type of electrolyte is one of the factors the voltage depends on.
misconceptions.misconception: The voltage is set entirely by the two metals; the electrolyte is only there to complete the circuit, so swapping it makes no difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The metals are the visible, obviously different parts of the cell, and students transfer the idea of a wire completing a circuit to the liquid, treating it as a passive connector.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the voltage is dependent upon a number of factors including the type of electrode and electrolyte. Both matter, so a cell with the same two metals in a different electrolyte can give a different voltage.

misconceptions.question: Will a bigger piece of metal as the electrode give a bigger voltage?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the type of electrode, not its size, that affects the voltage.
misconceptions.misconception: Using larger electrodes, or more electrolyte, gives a larger voltage, because there is more chemical there to react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that more reactant means more product, and wrongly transfer that quantity rule to voltage, which is not a quantity of anything produced.
misconceptions.correction: The factors named by the specification are the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte. Doubling the size of the electrodes does not double the voltage; a bigger cell may keep working for longer, but the voltage is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Can a simple cell be made from two electrodes of the same metal?
misconceptions.correct: No. A simple cell needs two different metals in contact with an electrolyte.
misconceptions.misconception: Any two pieces of metal dipped in an electrolyte will make a cell, so two copper strips work just as well as copper and zinc.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'electrode' is learnt from electrolysis, where two identical inert electrodes are normal, and that arrangement is carried over to cells without noticing the difference.
misconceptions.correction: A simple cell is made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Two identical electrodes have no difference in reactivity between them, so no voltage is produced.

misconceptions.question: Is a single cell a battery?
misconceptions.correct: No. A battery consists of two or more cells connected together in series.
misconceptions.misconception: Cell and battery mean the same thing, so the AA cell in a torch is a battery.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Shops and everyday speech call every portable power source a battery, and the chemical meaning of the word is never encountered outside science lessons.
misconceptions.correction: Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage. One cell on its own is a cell; joining cells in series makes a battery.

misconceptions.question: What do you gain by connecting cells in series?
misconceptions.correct: A greater voltage. The voltages of the cells add together.
misconceptions.misconception: Connecting cells in series gives more current but the voltage stays the same as one cell, because the cells take it in turns to push.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Current is the quantity students picture flowing round the circuit, so 'more cells' is read as 'more flow', and series and parallel connection are easily confused.
misconceptions.correction: Cells are connected in series in a battery to provide a greater voltage. Four 1.5 V cells in series give a battery voltage of 6.0 V.

misconceptions.question: Why does a non-rechargeable battery go flat?
misconceptions.correct: Because one of the reactants inside it has been used up, so the reactions stop.
misconceptions.misconception: The battery has run out of electrons, or run out of the electricity that was stored in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It follows from the picture of a cell as a store of electricity, and the phrase 'the battery is dead' suggests something inside has been emptied rather than reacted.
misconceptions.correction: In non-rechargeable cells and batteries the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up. Electrons are not consumed; they circulate. What runs out is a chemical reactant.

misconceptions.question: Are alkaline batteries rechargeable?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkaline batteries are the rechargeable ones, because they are sold as long-life and are more expensive than ordinary batteries.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Packaging uses 'alkaline' as a premium label, and students associate the extra cost and longer life with the rechargeable type they own.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable. Once a reactant inside has been used up the reactions stop and supplying an external current will not reverse them.

misconceptions.question: What does recharging actually do to a cell?
misconceptions.correct: The external current reverses the chemical reactions inside the cell.
misconceptions.misconception: Recharging pumps fresh chemicals, or fresh electricity, into the cell to replace what was used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recharging is compared with refuelling a car, an analogy in which something material really is added, and nothing visible enters a battery to contradict it.
misconceptions.correction: Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. The same atoms are still in the cell; the products are turned back into the reactants.

misconceptions.question: Can any flat cell be recharged if you connect it to a power supply?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only cells whose reactions can be reversed by the current are rechargeable.
misconceptions.misconception: Every cell can be recharged; you just need a charger, and the ones labelled non-rechargeable are labelled that way to make you buy more.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The mechanism of recharging is invisible, so 'putting the electricity back' seems like something that could be done to any cell.
misconceptions.correction: Recharging works only where the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. In a non-rechargeable cell such as an alkaline battery they are not, so it cannot be recharged.

misconceptions.question: In a magnesium and copper cell, which metal is the negative electrode?
misconceptions.correct: Magnesium, the more reactive metal.
misconceptions.misconception: The less reactive metal is the negative electrode, because the more reactive metal is the stronger one and so must be positive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Positive' is read as a value word meaning better or stronger, and students match it to the more reactive metal instead of following the electrons.
misconceptions.correction: The more reactive metal loses electrons more readily, so it is the negative electrode. In a magnesium and copper cell magnesium is negative and copper is positive.

misconceptions.question: Which pair of metals gives the biggest voltage?
misconceptions.correct: The pair furthest apart in the reactivity series.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals that are close together in the reactivity series give the biggest voltage, because they are the best match for each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect similar things to work well together, and 'close together' sounds like a stronger relationship than 'far apart'.
misconceptions.correction: The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage. Two metals next to each other in the reactivity series give only a small voltage, and two of the same metal give none.

misconceptions.question: Does a hydrogen fuel cell need recharging?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is supplied with fuel and oxygen or air from outside.
misconceptions.misconception: A fuel cell is a kind of rechargeable battery: it holds its fuel inside and has to be plugged in and recharged when that runs out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fuel cells are met as an alternative to batteries and are pictured as batteries, so students assume the fuel must be stored inside like the reactants of an ordinary cell.
misconceptions.correction: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air. The fuel is fed in from outside, so the cell keeps working as long as the supply continues; it is refuelled, not recharged.

misconceptions.question: Is the hydrogen in a fuel cell burned?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is oxidised electrochemically within the cell.
misconceptions.misconception: The fuel cell burns hydrogen, and the heat from the flame is turned into electricity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'fuel' is tied to combustion in every other context students meet, from fuels in 4.7 to power stations, so a flame is assumed.
misconceptions.correction: The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference. The oxidation happens at an electrode, so the electrons pass through the external circuit instead of the energy being released as heat in a flame.

misconceptions.question: Does a hydrogen fuel cell produce carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. The overall reaction produces water.
misconceptions.misconception: It burns a fuel, and burning fuels always makes carbon dioxide, so a fuel cell must give out carbon dioxide too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'fuel plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water' is learnt for hydrocarbons and applied to hydrogen, which contains no carbon at all.
misconceptions.correction: The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water. Hydrogen contains no carbon, so no carbon dioxide can be formed: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

misconceptions.question: Are hydrogen fuel cells simply better than rechargeable batteries?
misconceptions.correct: No. They have advantages and disadvantages, which is why they are a potential alternative.
misconceptions.misconception: Fuel cells only produce water, so they have no drawbacks and there is no reason to keep using batteries.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The single clean product is memorable and evaluation questions are answered by listing advantages only, so the other side of the comparison is never brought to mind.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen fuel cells offer a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries. An evaluation must give both sides: no recharging time and water as the only product, set against the difficulty of storing and distributing hydrogen safely and the need for a hydrogen supply.

misconceptions.question: At the negative electrode of a hydrogen fuel cell, does hydrogen gain or lose electrons?
misconceptions.correct: It loses electrons: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
misconceptions.misconception: The electrode is called negative, so electrons must be pushed onto the hydrogen there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In electrolysis the negative electrode is where positive ions gain electrons, and that rule is transferred to a cell without noticing that in a cell the electrode is negative because the reaction there releases electrons.
misconceptions.correction: In a fuel cell the fuel is oxidised, and oxidation is loss of electrons. Hydrogen loses electrons at the negative electrode, 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, and those electrons flow out into the circuit, which is what makes that electrode negative.

misconceptions.question: Is H₂ → 2H⁺ + e⁻ an acceptable half equation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The charges do not balance; it needs 2e⁻.
misconceptions.misconception: A half equation is right as long as the atoms balance, because the electrons are only added on afterwards to show what moved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is first taught as balancing atoms, and electrons look like an optional extra written at the end rather than a species that must be counted.
misconceptions.correction: In a half equation the total charge must balance as well as the atoms. H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ has zero charge on each side; written with e⁻ it does not, and is wrong.

misconceptions.question: Will two different metals in a beaker of pure water make a cell?
misconceptions.correct: No. The metals must be in contact with an electrolyte.
misconceptions.misconception: Any liquid will do, so long as both metals are dipped in it and joined by a wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The liquid is seen as a way of joining the two metals, and water is the default liquid, so its role as a source of free-moving ions is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: A simple cell is made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Pure water contains almost no free-moving ions; a salt solution such as sodium chloride solution is an electrolyte and works.

misconceptions.question: Do the cells in a battery share the total voltage between them?
misconceptions.correct: No. Their voltages add up to give a greater total.
misconceptions.misconception: The voltage of the battery is divided between the cells, so each cell in a four-cell battery only supplies a quarter of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet potential difference sharing between components in series in physics and apply that rule to the sources rather than to the components.
misconceptions.correction: Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage. Four 1.5 V cells in series give 6.0 V, not 0.375 V.

misconceptions.question: Do hydrogen and oxygen react in the fuel cell to give H₂O₂?
misconceptions.correct: No. The product is water, H₂O.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen is H₂ and oxygen is O₂, so the product must be H₂O₂ with two of each.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae are built by carrying the subscripts of the reactants across into the product, instead of from the combining ratio of the elements.
misconceptions.correction: The formula of a compound comes from the combining ratio, not from the reactant formulae. Water is H₂O, and the balanced overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

misconceptions.question: Does a hydrogen fuel cell split water into hydrogen and oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: No. It does the opposite: hydrogen is oxidised to produce water.
misconceptions.misconception: A fuel cell is electrolysis of water, so water goes in and hydrogen and oxygen come out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fuel cells are taught close to electrolysis and both involve electrodes and hydrogen and oxygen, so the direction of the change is reversed in memory.
misconceptions.correction: The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Electrolysis of water is the reverse change and it consumes electricity instead of producing it.

misconceptions.question: Which electrode of a fuel cell is oxidation at?
misconceptions.correct: The negative electrode, where hydrogen loses electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxidation happens at the positive electrode, because in electrolysis oxidation happens at the anode and the anode is positive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'oxidation at the anode' is learnt in 4.4.3 together with 'anode is positive', and the pair is carried into fuel cells, where the electrode that supplies electrons to the circuit is the negative one.
misconceptions.correction: In a hydrogen fuel cell the hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode, 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, and oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode, O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.

mcqs.stem: A chemical cell is connected to a bulb and the bulb lights. Where does the electricity come from?

options.text: From a reaction between the chemicals inside the cell
options.rationale: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity; the reaction happens once the circuit is complete.

options.text: From electricity stored in the cell when it was made
options.rationale: The everyday picture of a battery as a container of electricity waiting to be poured out.

options.text: From a supply of electrons held ready in the metal case
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a cell holds a stock of electrons that gradually runs out.

options.text: From the air, which reacts with the metal parts of it
options.rationale: Confuses an ordinary chemical cell with a fuel cell, which is supplied with oxygen or air from outside.

mcqs.stem: The voltage produced by a cell depends on a number of factors. Which of these is one of them?

options.text: The size of the two pieces of metal used as electrodes
options.rationale: More reactant is assumed to mean more voltage, transferring a quantity rule where it does not apply.

options.text: The type of metal used for each of the two electrodes
options.rationale: The specification names the type of electrode as one of the factors the voltage depends on.

options.text: How long the cell was stored before it was first used
options.rationale: Follows from picturing a cell as a store of electricity that leaks away while it sits on a shelf.

options.text: The length of the wire joining the cell to the circuit
options.rationale: A circuit feature outside the cell, picked by students who look at the whole circuit rather than the cell.

mcqs.stem: A cell made from zinc and copper in copper sulfate solution gives 1.1 V. The copper sulfate solution is replaced by sodium chloride solution. What happens to the voltage?

options.text: It stays at 1.1 V, because the two metals are unchanged
options.rationale: Treats the electrolyte as a passive connector and the metals as the only thing that matters.

options.text: It stays at 1.1 V, because the electrodes are the same size
options.rationale: Picks size as the controlling factor, so a change of liquid is judged to make no difference.

options.text: It changes, because voltage depends on the electrolyte used
options.rationale: The type of electrolyte is one of the named factors, so a different electrolyte can give a different voltage.

options.text: It falls to zero, because sodium chloride is not an electrolyte
options.rationale: Sodium chloride solution does contain free-moving ions, so the cell still works; this confuses it with pure water.

mcqs.stem: What is needed to make a simple cell?

options.text: Two pieces of the same metal in contact with an electrolyte
options.rationale: Carried over from electrolysis, where two identical electrodes are normal.

options.text: Two different metals joined together by a length of wire
options.rationale: Leaves out the electrolyte, so there is nothing for the metals to react with.

options.text: Two different metals dipped into a beaker of pure water
options.rationale: Any liquid is assumed to do, overlooking the need for free-moving ions.

options.text: Two different metals in contact with an electrolyte
options.rationale: This is exactly the arrangement the specification gives for a simple cell.

mcqs.stem: Which of these arrangements will produce a voltage?

options.text: Zinc and copper strips dipping into sodium chloride solution
options.rationale: Two different metals in contact with an electrolyte, which is what a simple cell requires.

options.text: Zinc and copper strips dipping into a beaker of pure water
options.rationale: The metals differ but pure water has almost no free-moving ions, so it is not an electrolyte.

options.text: Two copper strips dipping into copper sulfate solution
options.rationale: There is an electrolyte, but the two electrodes are the same metal, so no voltage is produced.

options.text: Zinc and copper strips held apart in air and joined by wire
options.rationale: Two different metals, but with no electrolyte in contact with them the cell is not complete.

mcqs.stem: What is a battery?

options.text: Another name for a single cell containing chemicals
options.rationale: Everyday speech uses battery for any single portable power source.

options.text: Two or more cells connected in series to give a greater voltage
options.rationale: The specification's definition: cells joined in series so that their voltages add.

options.text: Two or more cells connected in series to give a greater current
options.rationale: Current is the quantity students picture flowing, so more cells is read as more current.

options.text: A cell that can be recharged by an external electrical current
options.rationale: Describes a rechargeable cell rather than a battery, confusing two different distinctions.

mcqs.stem: Four identical 1.5 V cells are connected together in series to make a battery. What is the voltage of the battery?

options.rationale: Chosen by students who think series connection raises the current and leaves the voltage unchanged.
The voltage is divided by four, treating the cells as sharing a total rather than adding to one.
Cells in series add: 4 x 1.5 V = 6.0 V, which is the greater voltage a battery provides.
Only two of the four cells have been counted, a common slip when adding the cells up.

mcqs.stem: Why does a non-rechargeable cell eventually stop producing electricity?

options.text: The store of electrons inside it has all been given out
options.rationale: Electrons are pictured as a consumable stock rather than as circulating charge.

options.text: The electricity put in when it was made has been used up
options.rationale: Follows directly from the idea that a cell is filled with electricity at the factory.

options.text: The electrolyte has evaporated and can no longer conduct
options.rationale: A plausible physical failure, but not the chemical reason the specification gives.

options.text: One of the reactants inside it has been completely used up
options.rationale: The reactions stop when a reactant runs out, which is the specification's explanation.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about alkaline batteries is correct?

options.text: They are non-rechargeable, so they cannot be recharged
options.rationale: The specification states plainly that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.

options.text: They are rechargeable because they contain an alkali
options.rationale: The premium 'alkaline' label is associated with the rechargeable batteries students own.

options.text: They can be recharged by connecting a power supply
options.rationale: Assumes any cell can be recharged if a current is supplied to it.

options.text: They recharge themselves slowly if they are left unused
options.rationale: Extends the idea that recharging tops a cell back up, here with no charger at all.

mcqs.stem: Why can a rechargeable cell be recharged?

options.text: An external current pushes fresh chemicals into the cell
options.rationale: Recharging is modelled on refuelling, in which material really is added.

options.text: An external electrical current reverses the chemical reactions
options.rationale: This is the reason the specification gives for rechargeable cells being rechargeable.

options.text: An external current refills the cell with a store of electrons
options.rationale: Keeps the picture of a cell as an electron tank that can be topped up.

options.text: An external current warms the cell so the reaction restarts
options.rationale: Uses a rate idea, temperature, in place of the reversal of the reaction.

mcqs.stem: A rechargeable cell has gone flat and is connected to a charger. What happens inside the cell?

options.text: New reactants are supplied to the cell through the electrodes
options.rationale: The refuelling analogy again: something material is assumed to enter the cell.

options.text: Electrical charge is stored between the electrodes for later
options.rationale: Treats the cell as a container of electricity rather than of chemicals.

options.text: The products of the reaction are turned back into reactants
options.rationale: The current reverses the chemical reactions, re-forming the reactants that had been used up.

options.text: The electrolyte is replaced by a fresh conducting solution
options.rationale: A sealed cell exchanges nothing with the outside; only the chemical change is reversed.

mcqs.stem: Cells are made using a copper electrode and a second metal in the same electrolyte. The voltages are: magnesium 2.7 V, zinc 1.1 V, iron 0.8 V, tin 0.5 V. What do these data show?

options.text: Metals close together in the reactivity series give the biggest voltage
options.rationale: Students expect similar metals to pair well, and read 'close' as a stronger relationship.

options.text: The heavier the second metal is, the smaller the voltage produced
options.rationale: The data happen to fit this order, so a student matching a pattern rather than using chemistry picks it.

options.text: The more reactive the second metal, the smaller the voltage made
options.rationale: The trend read backwards, a common slip when a table is scanned from the bottom row upwards.

options.text: The bigger the difference in reactivity, the bigger the voltage
options.rationale: Magnesium is furthest from copper in reactivity and gives the largest voltage; tin is nearest and gives the smallest.

mcqs.stem: A simple cell is made from magnesium and copper in an electrolyte. Which electrode is the negative one?

options.text: Magnesium, because it is the more reactive of the two metals
options.rationale: The more reactive metal loses electrons more readily, so it becomes the negative electrode.

options.text: Copper, because the less reactive metal releases the electrons
options.rationale: The direction of electron loss is reversed, often because 'positive' is read as meaning stronger.

options.text: Whichever metal is the larger piece dipped into the liquid
options.rationale: Size is treated as the controlling factor instead of the type of metal.

options.text: Magnesium, because it is the lighter of the two metals used
options.rationale: Right electrode reached by the wrong route; density has nothing to do with the polarity.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is a valid reason for choosing a rechargeable battery instead of an alkaline battery?

options.text: Alkaline batteries need recharging more often than it does
options.rationale: Assumes alkaline batteries are rechargeable, which the specification states they are not.

options.text: It can be recharged and reused, so less waste is produced
options.rationale: The reactions are reversed by an external current, so one battery does the work of many.

options.text: Recharging adds new chemicals, so it will never wear out
options.rationale: The refuelling model of recharging, which also wrongly implies unlimited life.

options.text: It produces a higher voltage than an alkaline battery does
options.rationale: Voltage depends on the electrodes and electrolyte, not on whether a cell is rechargeable.

mcqs.stem: How is a hydrogen fuel cell kept working?

options.text: It is recharged from the mains when its fuel has run out
options.rationale: Treats the fuel cell as a rechargeable battery holding its reactants inside.

options.text: The hydrogen inside it is burned to heat the electrolyte
options.rationale: The word fuel is tied to combustion in every other context students meet.

options.text: Hydrogen and oxygen or air are supplied to it from outside
options.rationale: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air.

options.text: Its used electrolyte is drained off and topped up with new
options.rationale: Plausible maintenance, but it is the fuel and oxygen that are supplied, not the electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the fuel in a fuel cell is correct?

options.text: It is burned in oxygen, and the heat produced makes electricity
options.rationale: The combustion model of a fuel, with a flame and a heat engine assumed.

options.text: It is stored inside the cell and is used up as the cell works
options.rationale: Describes an ordinary chemical cell; a fuel cell is supplied from an external source.

options.text: It is split by an electric current into hydrogen and oxygen
options.rationale: Confuses the cell with electrolysis, which uses electricity instead of producing it.

options.text: It is oxidised electrochemically, producing a potential difference
options.rationale: The oxidation happens at an electrode, so the electrons transferred pass through the circuit.

mcqs.stem: What does the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell produce?

options.text: Water, from the oxidation of hydrogen
options.rationale: The overall reaction involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, from burning the fuel
options.rationale: The hydrocarbon combustion rule applied to a fuel that contains no carbon.

options.text: Hydrogen peroxide, from H₂ and O₂
options.rationale: The product formula is built by carrying the reactant subscripts straight across.

options.text: Oxygen, released at the electrode
options.rationale: Oxygen is a reactant here; it is a product in electrolysis, which is the reverse change.

mcqs.stem: Which equation shows the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?

options.text: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂
options.rationale: Balances only because the wrong product formula has been built from the reactants.

options.text: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
options.rationale: Hydrogen is oxidised to water and the equation balances: four H and two O on each side.

options.text: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂
options.rationale: The right species but the reverse change: this is the electrolysis of water.

options.text: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
options.rationale: The correct product, but the oxygen atoms are not balanced: two on the left, one on the right.

mcqs.stem: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell over a rechargeable battery?

options.text: It can be recharged far more quickly than a battery can be
options.rationale: Still treats the fuel cell as a battery, only a faster-charging one.

options.text: It produces a much higher voltage than any battery can give
options.rationale: Voltage is not the basis of the comparison the specification asks students to make.

options.text: It keeps working while fuel is supplied, with no recharging time
options.rationale: The fuel comes from an external source, so the cell is refuelled rather than left to recharge.

options.text: It stores much more electricity inside it than a battery does
options.rationale: Both devices are pictured as containers of electricity, one simply larger.

mcqs.stem: Which is a disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells compared with rechargeable batteries?

options.text: There are no disadvantages, so they will replace batteries
options.rationale: The single clean product is remembered and the other side of the evaluation is not.

options.text: They release carbon dioxide from the cell as they work
options.rationale: The combustion rule applied to hydrogen, which contains no carbon at all.

options.text: The water they produce has to be stored inside the cell
options.rationale: Plausible-sounding but wrong: the water formed leaves the cell rather than filling it.

options.text: Hydrogen is difficult to store and to distribute safely
options.rationale: A supply of hydrogen must be produced, stored under pressure and delivered, which batteries do not need.

mcqs.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode?

options.rationale: Hydrogen is oxidised, losing electrons; atoms and charge both balance.

options.text: H₂ → 2H⁺ + e⁻
options.rationale: Atoms balance but charge does not; the electron count has been overlooked.
Electrons placed on the left, so hydrogen is shown gaining them, which is reduction.
The reduction of hydrogen ions, written by a student recalling the cathode reaction of electrolysis.

mcqs.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which half equation shows the reaction at the positive electrode?

options.text: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
options.rationale: Oxidation written at the positive electrode, carried over from the anode in electrolysis.

options.text: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
options.rationale: Oxygen gains the electrons arriving from the circuit and is reduced to water; atoms and charge balance.

options.text: O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O
options.rationale: The right species and direction, but hydrogen atoms and charge are not balanced.

options.text: O₂ + 4H⁺ → 2H₂O + 4e⁻
options.rationale: Electrons put on the product side, so the equation shows a loss of electrons instead of a gain.
